newsitem.title: USA: Amazon.com prices offering above expectations.
newsitem.headline: Amazon.com prices offering above expectations.

text.p: Online book retailer Amazon.com Inc. said Wednesday its initial public offering of 3 million shares will be offered at $18 a share, slightly above expectations.
In a statement, the Seattle-based company said it granted to the underwriters an option to purchase up to 450,000 additional shares from the company for the purpose of covering over-allotments.
The move means Amazon.com will raise more than $54 million when its stock debuts on Thursday.
On Monday, lead underwriter Deutsche Morgan Grenfell raised the offering price to between $14 and $16 a share, reflecting healthy demand for the Internet book seller.
Amazon's offering has attracted considerable attention because the company has been one of only a handful of companies to successfully exploit the Internet as a vehicle for commerce.
The company offers more than 2.5 million titles and bills itself as the world's biggest bookstore.
On Monday, bookstore giant Barnes & Noble took issue with that description and filed a lawsuit against Amazon.com.
Barnes & Noble also launched its own Web site Tuesday, boasting more than 1 million available books, the vast majority of which were being offered at prices that undercut Amazon's.

At first blush, the fight between Amazon.com and Barnes & Noble hardly appears to be a fair one, pitting the 124-year-old chain, with more than 1,000 stores and $2.45 billion in sales last year, against a virtual rival that sold $15.7 million worth of books last year from its headquarters in a slightly run-down Seattle office building.

Amazon.com sales are rising exponentially -- the company posted $16 million in sales in the first quarter alone -- but the company warned in its prospectus that such growth rates are probably "not sustainable" and it expects to incur "substantial operating losses for the foreseeable future."
The company lost about $3 million in the first quarter and $6 million last year.
Nevertheless, the Amazon.com offering has been one of the year's hottest, especially since technology stocks have rebounded this month after slumping earlier in the year.

Investors are betting that with a cash infusion of some $40 million, Amazon.com founder Jeff Bezos, 33, will be able to capitalise on the buzz that has made his company one of the best-known names in Internet commerce.

But Amazon.com could have a tough time beating back Barnes & Noble and other rivals. Other booksellers also are dipping in to online waters, including Borders Group Inc., which is expected to announce its Internet plans soon.
